course.title: Java Programming Masterclass
course.description: Learn Java from scratch - setup, core syntax, object-oriented programming, collections, file I/O, and a complete Library Management System mini project.

lessons.title: Java Setup & Your First Program
lessons.body:
What is Java?

Java is a popular, general-purpose programming language used to build Android apps, web backends, games and enterprise software. It is platform independent: you write code once and run it anywhere a Java Virtual Machine (JVM) exists.

Step 1: Install the JDK

Download and install the Java Development Kit (JDK) from the official Oracle or OpenJDK website. The JDK includes the compiler (javac) and the runtime (java). Check your install in a terminal:

java -version
javac -version

Both commands should print a version number such as 17 or 21.

Step 2: Write your first program

Create a file named HelloWorld.java. The file name must match the public class name exactly, including capital letters.

public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, Java!");
    }
}

Every Java program starts running from the main method. System.out.println prints text to the screen and then moves to a new line.

Step 3: Compile and run

Compile the source file into bytecode, then run it:

javac HelloWorld.java
java HelloWorld

javac creates HelloWorld.class. java runs that class file (note: no .class in the run command). You should see Hello, Java! printed.

Key points

  • Install the JDK, which contains both the compiler (javac) and the runtime (java).
  • The file name must match the public class name exactly.
  • Every program starts at public static void main(String[] args).
  • Compile with javac, run with java, and every statement ends with a semicolon.

mcqs.q: Which command compiles a Java source file?
mcqs.why: javac is the Java compiler; it turns .java source files into .class bytecode files.

mcqs.q: What is the entry point of every Java program?
mcqs.why: The JVM looks for exactly public static void main(String[] args) and starts execution there.

mcqs.q: If your public class is named HelloWorld, what must the file be called?
mcqs.why: A public class must live in a file with the same name, including matching capital letters, ending in .java.

mcqs.q: What does System.out.println("Hi") do?
options: Prints Hi and moves to a new line
Prints Hi without a new line
mcqs.why: println prints the text and then a newline, so the next output starts on a fresh line.

mcqs.q: What does JDK stand for?
mcqs.why: The Java Development Kit bundles the compiler, runtime and tools needed to write and run Java.

mcqs.q: What file does javac produce from HelloWorld.java?
mcqs.why: The compiler produces bytecode in a .class file, which the JVM then runs.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: What does this program print?
tasks.answer: main runs first and println outputs the exact text Hello, Java! followed by a newline.
tasks.hint: println prints exactly what is inside the quotes.

tasks.title: Fix the missing semicolon
tasks.prompt: This program will not compile. Find and fix the bug.
tasks.answer: Every Java statement must end with a semicolon. The println line was missing one, so javac reports an error.
tasks.hint: Check the end of each statement inside main.

tasks.title: Fill in the main method
tasks.prompt: Complete the missing words so this program compiles and runs.
tasks.answer: The entry point must be declared public static void main(String[] args).
tasks.hint: The JVM needs a static method that returns nothing.

lessons.title: Variables, Data Types & Operators
lessons.body:
Variables

A variable is a named box that stores a value. You declare it with a type, a name, and optionally a starting value.

int age = 21;
double price = 99.50;
boolean isStudent = true;
char grade = 'A';
String name = "Siddartha";

Primitive data types

int stores whole numbers, double stores decimals, boolean stores true or false, and char stores a single character in single quotes. String is not a primitive type - it is a class - and its values use double quotes.

Operators

Java has arithmetic operators (+ - * / %), assignment operators (= += -=) and comparison operators (== != < >). Watch out for integer division:

public class Variables {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int age = 21;
        String name = "Siddartha";
        System.out.println(name + " is " + age);
        System.out.println(7 / 2);   // prints 3, not 3.5
        System.out.println(7.0 / 2); // prints 3.5
        System.out.println(10 % 3);  // prints 1 (remainder)
    }
}

When both operands of / are ints, Java drops the fractional part. Make one operand a double to get a decimal result. The % operator gives the remainder after division.

Key points

  • Declare a variable with a type, a name, and a value: int age = 21;
  • int is for whole numbers, double for decimals, boolean for true/false, char for one character.
  • String values use double quotes; char values use single quotes.
  • 7 / 2 is 3 in Java because int division drops the fraction - use 7.0 / 2 for 3.5.
  • % gives the remainder, so 10 % 3 is 1.

video.title: Learn Java 8 - Full Tutorial for Beginners

mcqs.q: What does 7 / 2 print in Java?
mcqs.why: Both operands are ints, so Java performs integer division and drops the .5, giving 3.

mcqs.q: Which type stores true or false?
mcqs.why: boolean is the type for the two values true and false.

mcqs.q: Which line correctly declares a decimal price?
mcqs.why: double stores decimal numbers; int cannot hold 9.99 and the other types are for characters and true/false.

mcqs.q: What is the value of x after int x = 5; x += 3;?
mcqs.why: x += 3 is shorthand for x = x + 3, so 5 + 3 = 8.

mcqs.q: What is 10 % 3 in Java?
mcqs.why: % gives the remainder: 10 divided by 3 is 3 remainder 1.

mcqs.q: Which is a valid String declaration?
mcqs.why: String is a capitalised class name and its value must be in double quotes.

tasks.answer: a / b is integer division, so 7 / 2 = 3. a % b is the remainder, 7 % 2 = 1.
tasks.hint: Remember: int / int drops the fraction, and % gives the remainder.

lessons.title: Conditionals & Loops
lessons.body:
if, else if, else

Conditionals let your program choose a path. Java checks each condition from top to bottom and runs the first branch that is true.

int marks = 75;
if (marks >= 90) {
    System.out.println("Grade A");
} else if (marks >= 60) {
    System.out.println("Grade B");
} else {
    System.out.println("Grade C");
}

Here 75 is not >= 90 but is >= 60, so it prints Grade B.

Comparing strings

Use .equals() to compare string contents. The == operator compares whether two variables refer to the same object, which is not the same as having equal text, so == on strings is unreliable.

String answer = "yes";
if (answer.equals("yes")) {
    System.out.println("Confirmed");
}

Loops

A for loop repeats a known number of times. A while loop repeats while a condition stays true, and a do-while loop always runs at least once because the condition is checked at the end.

public class Grades {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
            System.out.println("Count: " + i);
        }
        int n = 1;
        while (n <= 3) {
            System.out.println("While: " + n);
            n++;
        }
    }
}

The for loop prints Count: 1, Count: 2, Count: 3. The while loop does the same with While: as the prefix. Use break to exit a loop early.

Key points

  • if / else if / else runs the first branch whose condition is true.
  • Compare string contents with .equals(), never with ==.
  • for loops suit a known number of repetitions; while loops suit an unknown number.
  • do-while always runs at least once because its condition is checked last.
  • break exits a loop early.

flowchart.title: How an if-else decides a grade

mcqs.q: What is the correct way to check if two strings have the same text?
mcqs.why: .equals() compares the contents of strings; == compares object references, which can be false even for equal text.

mcqs.q: How many times does for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) run its body?
mcqs.why: i takes the values 0, 1 and 2, then the condition i < 3 fails at 3, so the body runs 3 times.

mcqs.q: How is a do-while loop different from a while loop?
options: It runs its body at least once
mcqs.why: do-while checks its condition after the body, so the body always executes once even if the condition starts false.

mcqs.q: What does break do inside a loop?
mcqs.why: break jumps out of the enclosing loop at once; continue is the keyword that skips to the next iteration.

mcqs.q: In if (marks >= 60) { ... } else { ... }, which branch runs when marks is 75?
mcqs.why: 75 >= 60 is true, so the if branch runs and the else branch is skipped.

mcqs.q: What is wrong with if (x = 5)?
options: It assigns 5 to x instead of comparing
mcqs.why: A single = assigns the value 5 to x; comparison needs ==. In Java this does not even compile for an int condition.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: What does this program print?
tasks.answer: i starts at 1 and the loop runs while i <= 3, printing Count: 1, then 2, then 3, before i becomes 4 and stops.
tasks.hint: Count how many values i takes from 1 to 3.

tasks.title: Fix the comparison
tasks.prompt: This condition does not compare - it assigns. Fix it.
tasks.answer: A single = assigns 5 to x and the if then has no boolean to test, so it fails to compile. == compares x with 5 and gives true.
tasks.hint: Comparison needs two equals signs.

tasks.title: Trace the while loop
tasks.prompt: Trace i step by step until the loop ends.
tasks.expected: i = 0, check 0 < 3 true, i = 1, check 1 < 3 true, i = 2, check 2 < 3 true, i = 3, check 3 < 3 false, prints 3
tasks.answer: Each pass checks i < 3 before incrementing. After three increments i is 3, the check fails, and 3 is printed.
tasks.hint: Follow the flowchart: check the condition, then run the body, then check again.

tasks.title: Fill in the loop condition
tasks.prompt: Complete the for header so the loop runs exactly 3 times.
tasks.answer: With i starting at 0, i < 3 gives the values 0, 1, 2 - exactly three runs. Using <= would give four.
tasks.hint: Starting at 0, which operator gives exactly three values?

lessons.title: Methods & Arrays
lessons.body:
Methods

A method is a named block of code that does one job. It can take inputs (parameters) and return a result. Methods keep your code organised and reusable.

public static int sum(int[] numbers) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++) {
        total += numbers[i];
    }
    return total;
}

public static means the method belongs to the class and can be called without creating an object. int is the return type - the method gives back an int. void would mean it returns nothing.

Arrays

An array stores a fixed number of values of the same type. Indexing starts at 0, so the first element is index 0 and the last is index length - 1.

public class ArraysDemo {
    public static int sum(int[] numbers) {
        int total = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++) {
            total += numbers[i];
        }
        return total;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] marks = {80, 90, 70};
        System.out.println("Total: " + sum(marks));
        System.out.println("First mark: " + marks[0]);
        System.out.println("How many: " + marks.length);
    }
}

This prints Total: 240, First mark: 80, How many: 3. Notice the loop condition is i < marks.length - using <= would try to read index 3, which does not exist, and crash with an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Key points

  • A method has a return type, a name, parameters, and a body; void means it returns nothing.
  • static methods can be called from main without creating an object.
  • Arrays hold a fixed number of values of one type; indexing starts at 0.
  • Use array.length and loop with i < length to avoid going past the end.
  • Reading past the last index throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

mcqs.q: Given int[] nums = {1, 2, 3}; what is nums[1]?
mcqs.why: Array indexing starts at 0, so index 1 is the second element, which is 2.

mcqs.q: What is nums.length for int[] nums = {1, 2, 3};?
mcqs.why: length is the number of elements in the array, which is 3.

mcqs.q: What happens when you read nums[3] from int[] nums = {1, 2, 3};?
mcqs.why: Valid indexes are 0 to 2; index 3 is past the end, so Java throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

mcqs.q: What does a void return type mean for a method?
mcqs.why: void means the method performs an action and gives back no value.

mcqs.q: Why can main call a static method directly?
mcqs.why: A static method belongs to the class itself, so it can be called without creating an object of the class.

mcqs.q: What is args in public static void main(String[] args)?
mcqs.why: args is a String array holding any words typed after the class name on the command line.

tasks.prompt: What does this program print?
tasks.answer: The loop adds 80 + 90 + 70 = 240, and marks[0] is the first element, 80.
tasks.hint: Add the three elements and remember indexing starts at 0.

tasks.title: Fix the off-by-one error
tasks.prompt: This loop crashes. Fix it.
tasks.answer: marks.length is 3 but the last valid index is 2. With <= the loop tries marks[3] and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; < stops at index 2.
tasks.hint: The last valid index is length - 1.

tasks.title: Fill in the return type
tasks.prompt: Complete the method header so it can return an int total.
tasks.answer: The method returns total, which is an int, so its return type must be int.
tasks.hint: What type is the value after return?

tasks.title: Trace the array sum
tasks.prompt: Trace total step by step.
tasks.expected: total = 0, i = 0 adds 80, total = 80, i = 1 adds 90, total = 170, i = 2 adds 70, total = 240
tasks.answer: Each loop pass adds one element: 0 + 80 = 80, then + 90 = 170, then + 70 = 240, and the loop ends when i reaches 3.
tasks.hint: Walk the loop one index at a time, updating total.

lessons.title: Object-Oriented Programming in Java
lessons.body:
Classes and objects

A class is a blueprint; an object is a real thing built from it. A class holds fields (data) and methods (behaviour). You create an object with the new keyword, which runs a constructor.

public class Student {
    private String name;
    private int age;

    public Student(String name, int age) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public void introduce() {
        System.out.println("Hi, I am " + name + ", age " + age);
    }
}

Constructors and this

A constructor has the same name as the class and no return type - not even void. It runs once when the object is created. Inside it, this.name means the object's own field, which lets you tell it apart from the parameter also called name.

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s = new Student("Sid", 21);
        s.introduce();
        System.out.println(s.getName());
    }
}

This prints "Hi, I am Sid, age 21" and then "Sid". Each object keeps its own copy of the fields, so two Student objects can hold different names.

Encapsulation

Marking fields private hides them from outside code. Other classes then use public getters (and setters) to read or change them. This protects the data - nobody can set a negative age directly, for example.

Key points

  • A class is a blueprint; an object is created from it with new.
  • A constructor has the class name and no return type; it runs when the object is created.
  • this.field refers to the object's own field, not a same-named parameter.
  • private fields plus public getters and setters is called encapsulation.
  • Each object keeps its own copy of the fields.

mcqs.q: Which keyword creates an object from a class?
mcqs.why: new allocates the object and runs its constructor, for example new Student("Sid", 21).

mcqs.q: What must a constructor's name be?
options: The same as the class name
The same as the first field
mcqs.why: A constructor is identified by having exactly the class name and no return type.

mcqs.q: Can code in another class read a private field directly?
options: No, it must use a public getter
mcqs.why: private hides the field outside its own class; a public getter method is the controlled way to read it.

mcqs.q: Which line correctly defines a class named Student?
mcqs.why: A class is declared with the keyword class followed by its name and a body in braces.

mcqs.q: What does this.name refer to inside a class?
mcqs.why: this points to the current object, so this.name is the object's field, distinct from a parameter also called name.

mcqs.q: How many objects does Student a = new Student("Sid", 21); Student b = new Student("Anu", 20); create?
mcqs.why: Each new expression creates a separate object, so two news make two independent Student objects.

s.introduce();
tasks.answer: new runs the constructor, storing Sid and 21 in the object's fields, and introduce() prints them.

tasks.answer: A constructor must be spelled exactly like the class name, with a capital S. A lowercase student looks like a method with no return type, which is a compile error.
tasks.hint: Constructors must match the class name exactly, including capitals.

tasks.prompt: Complete the line so a new Student object is created.
tasks.code: Student s = ___ Student("Sid", 21);
tasks.answer: The new keyword allocates the object and calls the constructor.
tasks.hint: Which keyword runs the constructor?

tasks.title: Trace two objects
tasks.prompt: Trace the fields of a and b and the output.
tasks.expected: a.name = Sid, a.age = 21, b.name = Anu, b.age = 20, prints 'Hi, I am Sid, age 21' then 'Hi, I am Anu, age 20'

tasks.hint: Objects do not share fields - trace each one separately.

lessons.title: Strings, Collections & Exception Handling
lessons.body:
Strings

Strings are objects with useful methods. Remember strings are immutable - methods like toUpperCase() return a new string instead of changing the original.

String word = "Java";
System.out.println(word.length());       // 4
System.out.println(word.toUpperCase());  // JAVA
System.out.println(word.charAt(0));      // J
System.out.println("java".equals("Java")); // false

length() counts characters, charAt(0) gives the first character, and equals() compares contents case-sensitively - "java" and "Java" are not equal.

ArrayList

Unlike arrays, an ArrayList can grow. It holds objects, so use wrapper types like Integer for numbers.

import java.util.ArrayList;

ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Sid");
names.add("Anu");
System.out.println(names.size()); // 2
System.out.println(names.get(0)); // Sid

Exceptions and try-catch

An exception is a runtime error, such as dividing by zero or parsing bad input. Wrap risky code in try and handle the problem in catch so the program keeps running.

public class StringsDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            int n = Integer.parseInt("abc");
            System.out.println(n);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            System.out.println("Not a number!");
        } finally {
            System.out.println("Done");
        }
    }
}

parseInt("abc") throws NumberFormatException, the catch block prints "Not a number!", and the finally block always runs, printing "Done".

Key points

  • String methods include length(), charAt(), toUpperCase(), substring() and equals(); strings are immutable.
  • Compare string contents with .equals() - it is case-sensitive.
  • ArrayList grows as you add items; use add(), get() and size().
  • try-catch lets a program survive a runtime error instead of crashing.
  • finally always runs, even when an exception is thrown.

video.title: Learn Java 8 - Full Tutorial for Beginners

mcqs.q: What does "Java".length() return?
mcqs.why: length() counts the characters J, a, v, a - four in total.

mcqs.q: What does "java".equals("Java") return?
mcqs.why: equals() is case-sensitive, and the lowercase j differs from the capital J.

mcqs.q: After list.add("A"); what is list.size() for a new empty ArrayList?
mcqs.why: An empty list has size 0; adding one element makes the size 1.

mcqs.q: Which block always runs, even if an exception is thrown?
mcqs.why: finally is designed for cleanup code that must run whether or not an exception occurred.

mcqs.q: What does Integer.parseInt("12") return?
mcqs.why: parseInt converts the text 12 into the integer value 12.

mcqs.q: What does "Hello".substring(1, 3) return?
mcqs.why: substring(1, 3) takes characters at indexes 1 and 2, which are e and l; the end index is exclusive.

tasks.prompt: What does this program print?
tasks.answer: equals is case-sensitive so Java and java differ, giving false; length counts 4 characters.
tasks.hint: Check the capital J in the first string versus the small j in the second.

tasks.title: Fix the crash
tasks.prompt: This program crashes on bad input. Fix it so it prints a friendly message instead.
tasks.code:
int x = 10 / 0;
System.out.println(x);
tasks.answer: Dividing by zero throws ArithmeticException at runtime. Wrapping the division in try and catching ArithmeticException lets the program print a message instead of crashing.
tasks.hint: Which exception does division by zero throw, and how do you catch it?

tasks.title: Fill in the catch
tasks.prompt: Complete the missing keyword so the error is handled.
tasks.answer: A catch block follows try and names the exception type it handles, here NumberFormatException.
tasks.hint: The block that handles the exception starts with this keyword.

tasks.title: Trace the ArrayList
tasks.prompt: Trace the size of the list and what is printed.
tasks.expected: size starts 0, after add A size 1, after add B size 2, prints 2 then B
tasks.answer: Each add grows the list by one. After two adds the size is 2, and get(1) returns the second element, B.
tasks.hint: Count the adds, then remember get() uses 0-based indexes.

lessons.title: File I/O & Mini Patterns
lessons.body:
Writing a file

Java can read and write files. PrintWriter writes text, and wrapping it in try-with-resources closes the file automatically, even if an error occurs.

import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.io.FileWriter;
import java.io.IOException;

public class FileDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("notes.txt"))) {
            out.println("Hello, file!");
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.out.println("Could not write file");
        }
    }
}

File operations can fail - a disk may be full or a folder may not exist - so Java forces you to handle IOException with a try-catch or a throws declaration.

Reading a file

Use a Scanner on a File object and loop while hasNextLine() is true. Each call to nextLine() returns one line of text.

import java.io.File;
import java.io.FileNotFoundException;
import java.util.Scanner;

try (Scanner in = new Scanner(new File("notes.txt"))) {
    while (in.hasNextLine()) {
        System.out.println(in.nextLine());
    }
} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
    System.out.println("File not found");
}

Mini patterns with nested loops

Nested loops build patterns. The outer loop picks the row; the inner loop prints the stars for that row.

for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    for (int j = 1; j <= i; j++) {
        System.out.print("*");
    }
    System.out.println();
}

Row 1 prints 1 star, row 2 prints 2, row 3 prints 3:

*
**
***

Key points

  • PrintWriter writes text to a file; Scanner reads it back line by line.
  • try-with-resources closes the file automatically - no manual close needed.
  • File work throws IOException or FileNotFoundException, so handle it with try-catch.
  • Nested loops make patterns: the outer loop is the row, the inner loop is the columns.
  • System.out.print() stays on the same line; println() moves to the next line.

flowchart.title: Reading a file line by line

mcqs.q: Which class writes text to a file in Java?
mcqs.why: PrintWriter has println methods that write text into a file; Scanner reads instead.

mcqs.q: What does try-with-resources do automatically?
mcqs.why: A resource declared in the try header is closed automatically when the block ends, even on error.

mcqs.q: In the star pattern, what does the outer loop control?
options: The number of stars in a row
mcqs.why: Each pass of the outer loop is one row; the inner loop decides how many stars that row gets.

mcqs.q: Which exception is thrown when Scanner cannot find the file to read?
mcqs.why: Opening a missing file with Scanner throws FileNotFoundException, a subclass of IOException.

mcqs.q: What does Files.readAllLines(path) return?
options: A List of Strings, one per line
mcqs.why: readAllLines reads the whole file and returns each line as one element of a List<String>.

mcqs.q: Which inner loop prints 1 star on row 1, 2 stars on row 2, and 3 on row 3?
mcqs.why: j <= i makes the inner loop run i times, so row i gets exactly i stars.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: What does this pattern code print?
tasks.answer: Row 1 runs the inner loop once (1 star), row 2 twice (2 stars), row 3 three times (3 stars), each followed by a newline.
tasks.hint: The inner loop runs i times for each row.

tasks.title: Fix the resource leak
tasks.prompt: This code writes a file but never closes it. Fix it.
tasks.code:
PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("notes.txt"));
out.println("Hello");
tasks.answer: An unclosed writer can lose data and leak a file handle. try-with-resources closes it automatically, and the catch handles the IOException that FileWriter can throw.
tasks.hint: Which construct closes a resource automatically?

tasks.title: Fill in the pattern bound
tasks.prompt: Complete the inner loop so row i prints i stars.
tasks.answer: j <= i runs the inner loop exactly i times, giving i stars on row i.
tasks.hint: Row 1 needs one star, so the loop must run when j equals i.

tasks.title: Trace the pattern loops
tasks.prompt: Trace i and j for the first two rows.
tasks.expected: i = 1, j runs 1, prints *, newline; i = 2, j runs 1 then 2, prints **, newline; i = 3 prints ***
tasks.answer: With i = 1 the inner loop runs once, with i = 2 it runs twice, and with i = 3 three times, building the triangle row by row.
tasks.hint: For each outer value, list the inner values.

lessons.title: Mini Project: Library Management System
lessons.body:
The project

You will build a console Library Management System that stores books, lets a user add a book, search by title, issue a book, return it, and list all books. It combines everything in this course: classes, ArrayList, loops, conditionals, strings and Scanner input.

Step 1: The Book class

Each book has a title and an availability flag. Fields stay private and are reached through getters and a setter.

public class Book {
    private String title;
    private boolean available;

    public Book(String title) {
        this.title = title;
        this.available = true;
    }

    public String getTitle() {
        return title;
    }

    public boolean isAvailable() {
        return available;
    }

    public void setAvailable(boolean available) {
        this.available = available;
    }
}

Step 2: The library and the menu

An ArrayList<Book> holds every book. A while loop shows a menu until the user chooses exit, and a switch runs the chosen action.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Scanner;

public class Library {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ArrayList<Book> books = new ArrayList<>();
        Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);
        int choice = 0;
        while (choice != 5) {
            System.out.println("1. Add book  2. Search  3. Issue  4. List books  5. Exit");
            choice = scanner.nextInt();
            scanner.nextLine();
            switch (choice) {
                case 1:
                    System.out.print("Title: ");
                    books.add(new Book(scanner.nextLine()));
                    break;
                case 4:
                    for (Book b : books) {
                        System.out.println(b.getTitle() + " - available: " + b.isAvailable());
                    }
                    break;
            }
        }
        scanner.close();
    }
}

Step 3: Searching and issuing

To search, loop through the books and compare titles with .equals() - never ==. To issue a book, check isAvailable() first, then call setAvailable(false). Returning a book sets it back to true.

Key points

  • Model each book as a Book object with a title and an available flag.
  • Store all books in an ArrayList<Book> so the library can grow.
  • A while loop plus a switch makes a menu that runs until the user exits.
  • Compare titles with .equals(), not ==.
  • Issue a book only when isAvailable() is true, then set it to false.

mcqs.q: Which collection is the best fit for storing the library's books?
mcqs.why: The library grows as books are added, and ArrayList<Book> holds Book objects and can grow; a fixed int array cannot.

mcqs.q: How should you check whether a book's title matches the search text?
mcqs.why: equals() compares string contents; == compares references and can miss a match.

mcqs.q: Which loop keeps the menu running until the user chooses Exit?
options: while loop with an exit condition
mcqs.why: A while loop repeats the menu while the choice is not Exit, which is exactly the repeated-until-exit behaviour needed.

mcqs.q: What type should a book's availability field be?
mcqs.why: Availability is a yes/no state, which is exactly what boolean models.

mcqs.q: How do you mark a book as issued using the Book class?
mcqs.why: available is private, so outside code must use the public setter setAvailable(false).

mcqs.q: Why is Book a separate class instead of storing titles in plain strings?
options: Each book bundles its title and availability together
Strings cannot be stored in a list
mcqs.why: A Book object keeps a title and its availability together, so the library can track each book's state instead of just a list of names.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: What does this program print?
tasks.answer: A new book starts available, so isAvailable() prints true. setAvailable(false) marks it issued, so the second print is false.
tasks.hint: What value does the constructor give available?

tasks.title: Fix the search
tasks.prompt: This search never finds a book that is actually there. Fix it.
tasks.answer: == compares object references, and the searched title is usually a different String object than the stored one, so the test fails even when the text matches. equals() compares the text itself.
tasks.hint: How do you compare string contents in Java?

tasks.title: Build the Library Management System
tasks.prompt: Build the complete console Library Management System: a Book class (title, available flag, constructor, getters, setter) and a Library main program with a menu loop. The menu must support: 1. Add book, 2. Search by title, 3. Issue a book, 4. Return a book, 5. List all books with availability, 6. Exit. Use an ArrayList<Book>, compare titles with .equals(), refuse to issue a book that is already issued, and close the Scanner when the program ends.
tasks.expected: Deliverable checklist: Book.java compiles with private fields, constructor, getters and setter; Library.java compiles and runs; menu repeats until Exit; adding a book then listing shows it as available; searching finds it by exact title; issuing it flips it to not available and issuing again is refused; returning it makes it available again; no == used for string comparison; Scanner is closed.
tasks.answer: Start with the Book class from this lesson, then build the Library main program one menu option at a time: add first, then list, then search with .equals(), then issue guarded by isAvailable(), then return. Test each option before adding the next.
tasks.hint: Build one menu option at a time and test it before moving on.
